name: Surface Area of a Right Circular Cone

scenes.animation: A birthday party: Zippy wears a paper party cap. He unrolls it flat on the table and it becomes a curved fan shape, not a triangle. Zippy gasps.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: My party cap unrolled into a fan! I thought cones were made of triangles.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: They're made of a sector of a circle. And that shape gives us the area formula.

scenes.animation: A right circular cone with labels: 'r = base radius', 'h = height (vertex to centre of base, at right angles)', 'l = slant height (vertex to any point on the base edge)'. The right triangle inside glows, and 'l² = r² + h²' writes itself.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: A right circular cone has a base radius r and a height h, measured from the vertex straight down to the centre of the base.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: The slant height l runs from the vertex to the edge of the base.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: r, h and l form a right triangle, so l squared equals r squared plus h squared.

scenes.animation: The unrolled sector is cut into many thin slices, each almost a triangle of height l. The slices line up; their bases add to 'arc length = 2πr'. Formula builds: 'Area = ½ × l × 2πr = πrl'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Cut the sector into many thin pieces. Each is nearly a triangle with height l.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Their bases together make the arc, which was the base circle, so they add up to 2 pi r.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Area is half into l into 2 pi r. So the curved surface area of a cone is pi r l.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Add the circular base, pi r squared, to get the total surface area: pi r into l plus r.

scenes.animation: Worked example on a chalkboard, line by line: 'r = 7 cm, h = 24 cm', 'l = √(7² + 24²) = √(49 + 576) = √625 = 25 cm', 'CSA = πrl = 22/7 × 7 × 25 = 22 × 25 = 550 cm²', 'TSA = πr(l + r) = 22/7 × 7 × (25 + 7) = 22 × 32 = 704 cm²'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Example: a cone has base radius 7 centimetres and height 24 centimetres. Take pi as 22 by 7.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Slant height is the root of 49 plus 576, which is the root of 625, or 25 centimetres.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Curved surface area is 22 by 7 into 7 into 25. The sevens cancel, leaving 22 into 25, which is 550 square centimetres.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Total surface area is 22 by 7 into 7 into 32, which is 704 square centimetres.

scenes.animation: A joker's cap and an ice-cream cone appear with a stamp 'Open cone → CSA only'. A closed conical toy gets 'Closed → TSA'. An 'EXAM TIP' card: 'Given h? Find l first.'

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: For my party cap, do I include the base?

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: No, a cap is open, so use only the curved surface area.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Exam tip: the formula needs slant height l. If the question gives height h, find l first.

scenes.animation: Recap board with the party cap: '1. l² = r² + h²', '2. CSA of cone = πrl', '3. TSA of cone = πr(l + r)'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Recap. One: slant height squared equals radius squared plus height squared.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Two: the curved surface area of a cone is pi r l.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Three: the total surface area is pi r into l plus r.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: Cap measured. Cake next!

name: Surface Area of a Sphere and a Hemisphere

scenes.animation: Zippy tries to gift-wrap a cricket ball with flat paper; the paper crinkles everywhere and Zippy ends up wrapped instead of the ball.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: Help! How much paper does a ball even need?

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: A ball is a sphere. There's a neat experiment to find its surface area.

scenes.animation: Activity animated step by step: a nail is pushed into a round ball, and string is wound neatly around it until the ball is covered; pins mark the start and end. The string is unwound and used to fill circles of the ball's radius: it exactly fills four circles.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Wind a string around a ball until it is fully covered. Then unwind it.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Now draw circles with the same radius as the ball, and fill them with the same string.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: The string exactly fills four circles. Each circle has area pi r squared.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: So the surface area of a sphere is 4 pi r squared.

scenes.animation: A sphere is sliced through its centre into two hemispheres. One half's curved dome glows: 'CSA = 2πr²'. Then its flat circular face glows: '+ πr²', giving 'TSA = 3πr²'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Cut a sphere through its centre and you get two hemispheres.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: The curved surface of a hemisphere is half of 4 pi r squared, which is 2 pi r squared.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: A solid hemisphere also has a flat circular face, pi r squared. So its total surface area is 3 pi r squared.

scenes.animation: Worked examples line by line: 'Sphere, r = 7 cm: 4 × 22/7 × 7 × 7 = 4 × 22 × 7 = 616 cm²'. Then 'Hemisphere, r = 21 cm: 22/7 × 21 × 21 = 22 × 3 × 21 = 1386', 'CSA = 2 × 1386 = 2772 cm²', 'TSA = 3 × 1386 = 4158 cm²'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Example: find the surface area of a sphere of radius 7 centimetres.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: 4 into 22 by 7 into 7 into 7. One seven cancels, leaving 4 into 22 into 7, which is 616 square centimetres.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Now a solid hemisphere of radius 21 centimetres. Pi r squared is 22 by 7 into 21 into 21, which is 1386.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Curved surface area is twice that, 2772 square centimetres. Total surface area is three times, 4158 square centimetres.

scenes.animation: A balloon inflates from radius 7 cm to 14 cm. A ratio card: 'r doubles → surface area × 4 (ratio 1 : 4)'. An 'EXAM TIP' card: 'Hollow bowl → CSA; solid hemisphere → TSA'.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: If I blow a balloon to double its radius, is the rubber surface double too?

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: No, four times. Area depends on r squared, so the ratio is 1 to 4.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Exam tip: a bowl is open, so use 2 pi r squared. A solid hemisphere uses 3 pi r squared.

scenes.animation: Recap board with the unwrapped ball: '1. Sphere: 4πr²', '2. Hemisphere CSA: 2πr²', '3. Solid hemisphere TSA: 3πr²'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Recap. One: the surface area of a sphere is 4 pi r squared.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Two: the curved surface area of a hemisphere is 2 pi r squared.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Three: the total surface area of a solid hemisphere is 3 pi r squared.

name: Volume of a Right Circular Cone

scenes.animation: An ice-cream cart. Zippy holds a cone and a cup shaped like a cylinder with the same base and height. The vendor charges the same price for both; Zippy squints suspiciously.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: Same base, same height, same price. But does the cone hold as much as the cup?

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Not even close. Let's measure.

scenes.animation: Activity animated: a hollow cylinder and a hollow cone with the same radius and height. The cone is filled with sand and poured into the cylinder: one third full, two thirds full, then exactly full after the third pour. Counter shows '1, 2, 3'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Take a hollow cylinder and a hollow cone with the same base radius and the same height.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Fill the cone with sand and empty it into the cylinder. It takes exactly three cones to fill the cylinder.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: So the volume of a cone is one third of the cylinder's volume: one third pi r squared h.

scenes.animation: Worked example on a chalkboard, line by line: 'r = 7 cm, h = 15 cm', 'V = ⅓ × 22/7 × 7 × 7 × 15', '22/7 × 49 = 154', '154 × 15 = 2310', '2310 ÷ 3 = 770 cm³'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Example: a cone has radius 7 centimetres and height 15 centimetres. Take pi as 22 by 7.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: 22 by 7 into 49 is 154. Then 154 into 15 is 2310.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: One third of 2310 is 770. So the volume is 770 cubic centimetres.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Next, a conical pit has a top diameter of 3.5 metres and a depth of 12 metres. Find its capacity in kilolitres.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: The radius is half the diameter, 1.75 metres. One third of 12 is 4, and 1.75 squared into 4 is 12.25.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: 22 by 7 into 12.25 is 22 into 1.75, which is 38.5 cubic metres.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: One cubic metre is one kilolitre, so the pit holds 38.5 kilolitres.

scenes.animation: An 'EXAM TIP' card: 'Diameter given? Halve it first', and a second card: '1000 cm³ = 1 L, 1 m³ = 1000 L = 1 kL'. Zippy crosses out '3.5' and writes '1.75'.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: I almost used 3.5 as the radius!

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Exam tip: if a diameter is given, halve it first. And remember, 1000 cubic centimetres make one litre.

scenes.animation: Recap board with the ice-cream cone: '1. Three cones fill one cylinder of same r and h', '2. Volume of cone = ⅓πr²h', '3. 1 m³ = 1 kL; 1000 cm³ = 1 L'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Recap. One: three cones fill a cylinder with the same base and height.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Two: the volume of a cone is one third pi r squared h.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Three: one cubic metre is one kilolitre, and 1000 cubic centimetres is one litre.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: Next time, I'm buying the cup.

name: Volume of a Sphere and a Hemisphere

scenes.animation: Zippy drops a big ladoo into a brimful glass of water; water spills into a tray below. He holds up the tray, amazed.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: My ladoo pushed out water! Is that its volume?

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Exactly. The water that overflows equals the volume of the sphere.

scenes.animation: Activity animated: spheres of different radii are dipped one at a time into a vessel filled to the brim; overflow water collects in a measuring cylinder. A table appears comparing overflow volumes with 'r³', and the formula 'V = 4/3 πr³' writes itself.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Dip spheres of different sizes into a vessel full of water, and measure the overflow each time.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: The overflow is always four thirds pi into the cube of the radius.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: So the volume of a sphere is four thirds pi r cubed.

scenes.animation: A sphere splits into two hemispheres; one is labelled 'V = ½ × 4/3 πr³ = 2/3 πr³'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: A hemisphere is half a sphere, so its volume is two thirds pi r cubed.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: Half a ladoo, half the volume. Fair enough, but I still want the whole one.

scenes.animation: Worked example on a chalkboard, line by line: 'r = 21 cm', 'V = 4/3 × 22/7 × 21 × 21 × 21', '21 ÷ 7 = 3 and 21 ÷ 3 = 7', 'V = 4 × 22 × 3 × 7 × 21', '= 88 × 441 = 38808 cm³'. Then 'Hemispherical bowl: 38808 ÷ 2 = 19404 cm³ ≈ 19.4 L'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Example: find the volume of a sphere of radius 21 centimetres.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Four thirds into 22 by 7 into 21 into 21 into 21. One 21 cancels the 7, leaving 3. Another 21 cancels the 3, leaving 7.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Now we have 4 into 22 into 3 into 7 into 21. That is 88 into 441, which is 38808 cubic centimetres.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: A hemispherical bowl of the same radius holds half of that, 19404 cubic centimetres, or about 19.4 litres.

scenes.animation: Two balls: radius r and radius 2r. A ratio card flips: '(2r)³ = 8r³ → volume × 8'. An 'EXAM TIP' card: 'Volume: r³ and cm³; surface area: r² and cm²'.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: So if I double the radius, the volume doubles?

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: No. Two cubed is eight, so the volume becomes eight times.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Exam tip: volume uses r cubed and cubic units. Surface area uses r squared and square units. Don't mix them.

scenes.animation: Recap board with the ladoo: '1. Volume of sphere = 4/3 πr³', '2. Volume of hemisphere = 2/3 πr³', '3. Radius × 2 ⇒ volume × 8'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Recap. One: the volume of a sphere is four thirds pi r cubed.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Two: the volume of a hemisphere is two thirds pi r cubed.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Three: doubling the radius makes the volume eight times bigger.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: An eight-times ladoo. Now that's a Diwali plan!
